what_its_for: Fedratinib is used to treat adults with a blood cancer called myelofibrosis. This includes patients who have a new diagnosis or whose disease came back or did not respond to a similar medicine called ruxolitinib. It works by blocking certain proteins (called JAK2 kinases) that help the cancer cells grow, which can help shrink an enlarged spleen and relieve symptoms like night sweats, itching, and bone pain.
how_to_take: Take fedratinib by mouth once a day, with food. Swallow the capsules whole — do not open, crush, or chew them. Taking it with a meal or snack (especially one that contains food) helps reduce stomach upset. Try to take it at the same time every day to keep a steady level of medicine in your body. If you vomit after taking your dose, do NOT take another dose that day — just wait until your next scheduled dose.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 400 mg (four 100 mg capsules) taken once daily. Your doctor may lower your dose if you have side effects or kidney problems. Always take the exact dose your doctor prescribes. Do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and it has been less than 12 hours since your scheduled time, take it as soon as you remember with food. If it has been more than 12 hours, skip the missed dose completely and take your next dose at your regular time the next day. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store fedratinib capsules at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Store them in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused or expired capsules.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while taking this medicine, as it can increase the amount of drug in your blood and worsen side effects. Tell your doctor about ALL other medicines, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you take, because many drugs can interact with fedratinib. Be careful with alcohol, as it may increase dizziness or stomach problems. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or confused. Do not start any new medicines without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience any of the following: confusion, memory problems, trouble speaking, seizures, or any change in your thinking (these could be signs of a rare but serious brain condition called Wernicke's encephalopathy); severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that does not get better; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; unusual bleeding or bruising; signs of serious infection such as fever, chills, or body aches; extreme tiredness or shortness of breath (which could signal low blood counts). Also tell your doctor if you develop numbness or tingling in hands or feet.
when_it_works: Most patients begin to notice improvements within the first 4 to 6 weeks of treatment, such as a smaller spleen or relief of symptoms. Your doctor will check your response to the medicine after about 6 months. Some improvements, like changes in blood counts, may take several months to become noticeable. Continue taking the medicine as directed even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Fedratinib can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 month after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should also use contraception during treatment and for 1 month after. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Kidney or liver problems: Your dose may need to be adjusted if you have moderate or severe kidney disease or liver problems — be sure your doctor knows your full medical history. Thiamine (Vitamin B1) levels: Your doctor will check your thiamine (vitamin B1) levels before and during treatment, and may prescribe a supplement, because this drug can lower your thiamine levels and cause a serious brain condition if left untreated. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects, so close monitoring is important.
